Before you build: write a useful software brief

A clear brief turns a broad idea into a more useful first conversation.

KS Digital BD · 5 min read

Start with the problem

Describe what is difficult today. “We enter the same order three times” is more actionable than “we need a modern system.” Include the people affected and the cost in time or effort.

Name the users

List who will use the product and what each person needs to accomplish. Separate customers, operational staff, managers and administrators where their needs differ.

Prioritise the first release

Choose the few workflows the first release must support. Keep future ideas in a separate list so they do not hide the core objective.

Describe your existing tools

Mention spreadsheets, websites, accounting tools and any data you expect to migrate. Integration requirements influence both scope and testing.

Agree what done means

For each core workflow, describe an observable result. For example: a staff member can create an order, update its status and find it again in the order history.

Bring constraints to the conversation

State your budget range, target date, available content and internal decision makers. These details help shape a realistic proposal.

These notes support project planning. Final requirements, pricing and responsibilities are agreed for each project.

Custom or ready-made software? Start with fit.

Choose an approach by comparing workflows, flexibility, ownership and ongoing effort.

KS Digital BD · 4 min read

Map the workflow first

List the tasks you need to support and the requirements that cannot change. A standard tool may fit a common process; a distinctive workflow may need configuration or custom development.

Compare the full cost

Look beyond the initial build or subscription. Consider data migration, setup, training, hosting, support and changes over time.

Check integrations and exports

Understand how your data moves between tools. Ask what can be exported, which formats are supported and how access works when a contract ends.

Understand responsibility

For custom work, agree source ownership, documentation, deployment access and maintenance. For a hosted product, review the provider’s service and data terms.

Test the important journeys

Use a small set of representative workflows to assess each option. A practical walkthrough is more informative than a long feature list.

Keep the decision proportionate
